unit.title: Perform manual metal arc welding process to AWS specification (Low carbon steel sheet)

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to weld thin low carbon steel sheet with manual metal arc welding (MMAW) to an AWS code and a welding procedure specification (WPS). You will learn how sheet differs from plate, how to choose electrodes, current and polarity, how to fit up and weld sheet joints in all positions, and how to make arc spot and stitch welds. You will also control distortion, inspect and test sheet welds, keep the records, and lead others on sheet work.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **MMAW of low carbon steel sheet** to the AWS code the Centre uses and a **welding procedure specification (WPS)**. AWS publishes a separate structural welding code for sheet steel (AWS D1.3), because sheet behaves differently from plate.

Sheet steel is everywhere in Jamaican fabrication: steel roof and floor deck on commercial buildings, cold-formed purlins and girts, electrical enclosures and meter boxes, cabinets, ducts, hoods, machine guards, truck bodies and doors. Arc welding thin sheet is harder than plate: it burns through easily, buckles, and is often oily or coated. Working to a sheet WPS is how a welder gets sound, flat, consistent work.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees and welders who already weld plate with MMAW and now work to a code on sheet, check other people's work and lead small jobs.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at Level 3
rows: Work to the code and the WPS
Read a sheet WPS, keep inside its ranges, and know when a change needs a new procedure or test.
Control burns, sharp edges, coated-sheet fumes, falls and shock on deck, and fire in ceilings and roofs.
Pick electrode type and size, current and polarity for the sheet thickness and position.
Measure the sheet, clean it, and fit butt, lap, tee, corner and flare joints with the right gap, tacks and backing.
Hold a short arc, travel steadily, and weld flat, horizontal, vertical (up or down) and overhead without burn-through.
Make arc spot and stitch welds
Join sheet to supports with arc spot welds and intermittent welds to the drawing.
Keep heat input low, sequence the welds, clamp and back the work.
Find sheet defects, run bend and peel tests, check flatness, and record the work.
Check qualifications, run a trial piece, coach and supervise.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the WPS, qualification, safety, electrodes, joints, arc spot welds, technique, positions, distortion, testing and records.
A **written paper**: short answers (exact terms such as weld washer, flare-bevel, PQR, DCEN, oil canning, 3G and 4F) with calculations, and longer answers explaining methods, tests and plans.

**Group practical tasks**: butt and lap joints in 2 mm sheet to a WPS (flat over a backing bar and vertical-down), with bend and break checks; and a sheet panel fixed to an angle frame with arc spot and stitch welds, peel tests and a flatness check.

blocks.note: Most marks are lost by treating sheet like plate. Learn the sheet habits: small electrode, low current, short arc, quick steady travel, close tacks, short runs.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Sheet steel, the code and the WPS

blocks.p: The AWS sheet steel code covers thin steel, up to about **4.8 mm** (3/16 in); the structural plate code covers steel from about 3 mm up. Most sheet jobs are 0.6–3 mm. Sheet comes flat, coiled or **cold formed** into sections (channels, Z and C purlins, deck profiles) with rounded bends.

**Low carbon (mild) steel** has a low carbon content (about 0.25 % or less). It welds easily, does not harden much as it cools, and has little risk of cracking, so preheat is rarely needed. The problems on sheet come from its **thinness** and its **surface**, not from its chemistry.

Sheet is often ordered by **gauge**. The higher the gauge number, the **thinner** the sheet, and gauge tables differ for plain and galvanised sheet. Always measure the real thickness in millimetres with a caliper or micrometer before you set up.

head: Surface
Problem in welding
What to do
rows: Degrease the weld area before welding
Zinc fume (metal fume fever), porosity, spatter
Remove from the weld area if the WPS allows; extraction; repair the coating after
Remove it from the weld area unless the WPS was qualified with that primer

ul: The **process** (MMAW), the steel, and the **thickness range** covered. Settings that suit 3 mm sheet burn straight through 1 mm, so a WPS is only good for the range it states.
The **joint types** and fit-up: gaps, overlaps, backing.
The **electrode** class and size, **current range** and **polarity**.
The **positions** and the direction of vertical welding (up or down).
Weld sizes, stitch lengths and spacing, and the welding sequence.
Cleaning, and the inspection and tests required.

head: Record
What it is
What it proves
rows: The written instructions for making the weld
How the weld must be made
The record of the test welds and test results that support a WPS
The record of a welder's test and the range it covers
What that welder is qualified to weld: process, thickness range, joint types and positions

ul: A welder tested only on plate may not be qualified for sheet, and a test in the flat position generally does not cover vertical or overhead. Check the WPQ against the job.
A qualification can **lapse**: under AWS codes, commonly if the welder has not used the process for six months. Then a retest is needed.
Changing an important variable (for example an electrode of a different AWS class, or a thickness outside the range) can need a new or re-tested WPS. Ask before changing anything.

blocks.note: Before production, weld a **trial piece** to the WPS and check it. It proves the settings on your machine, your sheet and your joint, and it becomes the sample everyone works to.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Hazard
Why sheet work is different
Controls
rows: Thin sheet gets hot through in seconds, and burn-through drops molten metal underneath
Check below the work for people and anything that burns
Sheet edges and offcuts are razor sharp
Offcuts straight into the scrap bin
Sheet is often galvanised, primed or oily
Local extraction close to the arc
Respirator for metal fume where extraction is not enough
On deck, roofs and enclosures, the welder kneels, sits or lies on steel that is part of the welding circuit
Sound leads; work clamp close to the weld
Deck and roof work is at height, near open edges and holes
Edge protection, or a harness clipped to a proper anchor
Deck fixed before anyone walks on it
Sparks and burn-through fall into ceilings, cavities and onto goods below
Check above and below; remove or cover what burns
Extinguisher at hand; fire watch during and after

blocks.p: Zinc burns off a galvanised sheet as white fume. Breathing it causes **metal fume fever**: shivering, fever, aches and sickness a few hours later, like flu. Check what the coating is before you start, remove it from the weld area if the WPS allows, weld with extraction, keep your head out of the plume, and wear a suitable respirator if the extraction is not enough. Repair the coating afterwards with zinc-rich paint, as the job asks.

blocks.h: Working on steel deck and roofs

ul: Plan the access and the **fall protection** before anyone goes up: edge protection, or harnesses clipped to proper anchors.
Keep leads tidy and tied off; a trailing lead on a roof is a trip and a pull towards the edge.
The whole deck is part of the welding circuit. Stay dry, kneel on an insulating mat and use a VRD where fitted.
Look below the deck before you strike: sparks and burn-through fall onto whatever is there.
Galvanised deck needs fume control even outdoors: stand upwind and use extraction or a respirator.

blocks.note: Under the midday sun a steel roof deck in Kingston or Montego Bay gets too hot to kneel on and can cause heat exhaustion. Start early, take shade breaks, drink water often, and keep electrodes in their packet out of the sun and the dew.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Hot work in ceilings and enclosed spaces

flow: Get a hot-work permit from the person in charge of the building
Check above and below the work: ceiling voids, cables, insulation, stock and people
Remove or cover anything that can burn; put a fire blanket where sparks will fall
Have an extinguisher at hand and a fire watcher in place
Weld, then keep the fire watch for the time the permit gives (often at least 30–60 minutes)
Check again before you sign off the permit

sections.title: Electrodes, current and polarity for sheet

blocks.p: For low carbon steel sheet, **E6013** (rutile) is the usual electrode. Its soft, smooth arc and shallow penetration suit thin metal, it runs on AC or DC, and its slag is easy to remove. The WPS names the class; use exactly that class.

head: Electrode
Character
On sheet
rows: Soft, quiet arc; shallow to medium penetration; neat bead
Digging arc; deep penetration; fast-freezing pool
Used by some procedures on dirty or galvanised work, but they burn through thin sheet easily
Strong, tough welds; needs a very short arc and dry storage
Harder to control on thin sheet; used where the WPS requires it

blocks.note: These are typical figures only. **The WPS current range rules**: set within it, start low on sheet, test on scrap of the same sheet and joint, and adjust in small steps. Follow the electrode maker's instructions and your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: An electrode that is too big needs too much current for the sheet, makes a pool too big to control and burns through.
On sheet, work in the **lower part** of the WPS range, and use travel speed to control the heat.
When joining sheets of different thickness, set the current for the **thinner** one, but aim the arc at the **thicker** one so the pool washes onto the thin edge.
Vertical and overhead welds usually need a little less current than flat.

head: Polarity
Where the heat goes
On sheet
rows: More heat into the work: deeper penetration
Used when the WPS calls for it
More heat into the electrode: it melts faster with shallower penetration
Puts **less heat into the sheet**: useful on thin sheet if the electrode maker and the WPS allow it
Fine for E6013; no arc blow

blocks.p: The dial on a machine is a guide, not a measurement. Where the WPS gives a range, a **clamp meter** (tong tester) round the electrode lead, or the machine's own display, shows the real welding current. A leader spot-checks the current at each station, especially on a long production run.

blocks.note: A short arc is even more important on sheet than on plate. A long arc wanders, spreads heat over a wider area, gives porosity and undercut, and makes the edges of a lap joint melt back.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Measure the sheet with a caliper and check it is inside the WPS thickness range.
Degrease and clean the weld area, both faces, about 25 mm back from the joint.
Deburr cut edges and check them for straightness: a wavy edge gives a gap that varies along the seam.

head: Joint
Where it is used
Main point to watch
rows: Joining sheets edge to edge in panels and ducts
Clean edges set close together (only the small gap the WPS allows), tacked often, often over a backing bar
Do not melt away the top edge: that cuts the throat and weakens the weld
Favour the thicker part so the thin one does not burn back
An open corner burns through easily: use a half-open or closed corner and low current
The turned-up edges melt down to form the weld
Where the rounded bend of a formed section meets a flat face
Fuse into the bottom of the curved groove and fill it to the size on the drawing
As flare-bevel: fuse the root and fill the groove

head: Corner type
How it is fitted
On sheet
rows: Edges meet point to point, leaving a V outside
Fills well on thicker sheet, but thin edges burn away
One sheet set back half its thickness
Gives a ledge to weld onto; less burn-through
One sheet overlaps the edge of the other
Least burn-through; good for thin enclosures

blocks.p: A **backing bar** is clamped under a butt joint. A **copper** bar draws heat away and supports the root so the pool does not drop through; it is not welded in and comes off afterwards. A **steel** backing strip, where the WPS allows it, is welded in and stays.

blocks.note: Never let the arc touch a copper backing bar. Copper melted into a steel weld can make it crack. Keep the bar clean and the joint closed tight onto it.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Tack **closely**: thin sheet moves with heat far more than plate. Spacing of about 25–50 mm is common on thin sheet; follow the WPS.
Tack from the **middle outwards**, or alternate ends, so the gap does not close up or open as you go.
Keep tacks small and fully fused, and fill their craters.
Clamp the sheet flat to the bench or jig while tacking.
**Short, steady arc**: about the core wire diameter or a little less.
**Quick, steady travel** with stringer beads. Do not weave wide: it spreads heat and burns through.
Watch the pool, not the electrode: if it starts to grow or sink, speed up, steepen the travel angle a little or break the arc briefly.
**Strike in the joint**, never on the sheet beside it. On thin sheet a stray arc strike can leave a hole or a hard spot.
Fill every **crater** before you lift away: an open crater can crack.
Restart just ahead of the crater on the joint line, then come back to fill it.

head: AWS position
Groove (butt) weld
Fillet weld
rows: 2F: one sheet flat, one upright (or a lap laid flat on the bench)
3G: sheets upright, weld runs up or down
3F: weld runs up or down the joint

head: Position
How to weld sheet
rows: Over a backing bar where possible; a steady, slightly hotter run is possible because the sheet supports the pool
Aim the arc at the lower (thicker or flat) sheet and let the pool wash up to the top edge; if the top edge melts back, the arc is aimed too high

Where the WPS allows: lower current, electrode pointing slightly up the joint, fast travel so the pool stays small. Quick travel means less heat in the sheet. Not for thicker sections, where it can leave lack of fusion
Where the WPS calls for it: small runs, a slight pause at the edges, no wide weave
Less current, very short arc, small quick stringer runs. Stand to the side, with cap, collar and sleeves done up

blocks.note: If a test or job piece burns through in a regular pattern (for example every 100 mm or so), look at where you paused, restarted or slowed down. Heat builds up wherever the arc stays longer.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Stop and let the area cool
Clean the edges of the hole and remove slag
Clamp a backing bar behind it if you can
At low current, fill from the edges inwards in short dabs, letting each one freeze
Dress the repair, check it, and record it on the job sheet

sections.title: Arc spot welds and stitch welds

blocks.p: An **arc spot weld** (sometimes called a puddle weld) joins sheet, usually steel deck, to the steel member under it. The arc burns through the top sheet with **no hole made first**, and the weld fuses into the support below. A **plug weld** is different: it is made in a hole drilled or punched first.

flow: Press the sheet **tight** onto the support at the marked spot; a gap lets the arc burn a hole without fusing into the support
Hold the electrode upright, strike the arc and burn through the top sheet
Move the electrode in a small circle to build up a round weld of the size the WPS gives, fused into the support all round
Fill the crater, chip the slag, and check the weld

ul: On very thin deck the WPS may call for a **weld washer**: a thin steel washer laid on the sheet so the weld is made through it and the thin sheet does not burn away round the weld.
Check each weld by eye: round, of the **visible size** the WPS gives (measured with a rule or gauge), fused all round its edge, no cracks or burnt-away sheet.
Before production, make arc spot welds on lapped test pieces and **peel test** them.

head: Peel test result
What it shows
rows: A button of weld tears out of the sheet, leaving a hole in it
Good: the weld is stronger than the sheet round it
The sheets part at the weld with a smooth, flat face and no torn metal
Fail: the weld did not fuse properly into the lower piece
The weld splits through its middle
Fail: weak, porous or cracked weld metal

blocks.p: An **arc seam weld** is a run made through the top sheet into the support along a line, rather than at a spot. It is made and checked in the same way.

On sheet, a continuous weld is often not needed and would put in too much heat. The drawing calls for **intermittent welds** written as length–pitch: **40-120** means welds 40 mm long, spaced at 120 mm **centres** (centre of one to centre of the next).

head: Question
How to work it out
Example for 40-120
rows: Number of welds on a seam (a weld at each end)
Approximate number on a long seam

blocks.note: Weld the stitches in a planned order, not one after another along the seam: for example every second stitch first, then the ones between, so the heat is spread.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Every weld shrinks as it cools. Thin sheet is not stiff enough to resist the pull, so it bows, buckles and twists. The more heat goes in, the worse it gets.

head: Kind of distortion
What you see
rows: A flat panel bulges and pops in and out when pressed, like the lid of a tin
A long seam or edge curves along its length
Sheets close up about the weld
The joint ahead of the weld moves as heat travels along it

head: Method
How it helps
rows: Small electrode, low current within the WPS range, quick travel, stringer beads
No bigger than the drawing asks; stitch welds where they are allowed
Holds the edges in line and stops the gap moving
Hold the sheet flat and draw heat away; leave clamped until cool
Each short run is welded **back towards** the end of the last one, while the overall progress goes forward, so heat and shrinkage are spread
Short runs at spaced points along the seam, filling the gaps later
Welds on opposite sides or ends in turn; work from the centre outwards
Folds, swages or a frame make a panel stiffer so it resists the pull

blocks.p: The plan that sets the order and direction of the welds on a panel is the **welding sequence**. Write it on the job sheet so everyone welds the panels the same way.

blocks.note: Distortion is far easier to prevent than to correct on sheet. Spot heating and hammering on a dolly can take out small buckles, but only as the supervisor directs: overdone, they make a panel worse.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Inspection, testing, records and leading the work

head: Defect
What it looks like on sheet
Usual causes
rows: Current too high; pausing or slow travel; gap too wide; electrode too big
The top edge of a lap joint melted away
Arc aimed at the top edge; long arc; too much current
Current too high; long arc; wrong angle; travel too fast
Weld sitting on the sheet without melting into it
Current too low; arc aimed wrongly; dirty sheet
Oil, zinc, primer, damp electrodes, long arc
Small cracks at the end of a run
Arc broken without filling the crater
Small burnt spots or holes away from the weld
Too much heat; poor sequence; not clamped

blocks.p: On sheet, small faults matter more than on plate. A 0.5 mm deep undercut is nothing on 12 mm plate but takes away a third of a 1.5 mm sheet. **Cracks are always rejected.**

ul: Check sizes against the drawing, squareness by diagonals, and **flatness** with a straight edge at marked points, recording the readings.
Check stitch lengths and spacing, and fillet sizes with a gauge.
Check arc spot welds for size and edge fusion.

head: Test
How
What it shows
rows: A strip across a butt weld is bent round a **former (mandrel)** of a set size, so every strip is bent the same way
Fusion and soundness: no cracks or openings beyond what the code allows
Lapped sheets joined by arc spot or fillet welds are prised or twisted apart
Whether the weld pulls a button out of the sheet
A lap or fillet joint is broken open in a vice
Fusion into the root and both sheets
A cut section is smoothed and etched

ul: Record the electrode class, size and batch, the current and polarity, the welder and the date for each batch of work, so a fault found later can be traced and put right.
Number each item and record its inspection results.
Mark faults on the job in paint, write them on a non-conformance note, agree the repair, and re-inspect after it.
Read the drawings and the WPS; list the sheet, electrodes and consumables.
Check each welder's WPQ covers the thickness, joints and positions, and that it has not lapsed.
Use a jig so every item is the same, and weld a **trial piece** to the WPS before production.
Write the settings and sequence on a card at each station, and spot-check the current with a clamp meter.
Coach welders who carry plate habits onto sheet: show them the sheet WPS range and let them practise on scrap of the same sheet.
Inspect and record each item; report quantities, faults and lessons at the end.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain why sheet is harder to weld than plate and how a sheet WPS deals with each problem.
I can explain WPS, PQR and WPQ, and when a qualification lapses or a WPS needs re-testing.
I can convert gauge to millimetres and always measure the real thickness.
I can control burns, cuts, coated-sheet fumes, shock on deck, falls and fire in hot work.
I can choose the electrode, size, current and polarity for a sheet job and check the current.
I can fit butt, lap, tee, corner and flare joints, use backing bars safely and tack sheet.
I can weld sheet flat, horizontal, vertical (up or down) and overhead without burn-through.
I can mend a burn-through.
I can make and check arc spot welds, and use weld washers where the WPS asks.
I can read and work out intermittent weld sizes, gaps and totals.
I can control distortion with heat input, sequence, clamping and backing.
I can inspect sheet welds, run bend and peel tests and check flatness.
I can keep records that let a fault be traced.
I can check qualifications, run a trial piece and coach welders on sheet.

terms: Arc spot weld
A round weld made through the top sheet into the support, with no hole made first; also called a puddle weld
Arc seam weld
A line weld made through the top sheet into the support
Backing bar
A bar under a butt joint that supports the root; copper bars draw heat away and are removed
Back-step welding
Welding short runs, each back towards the last, while the work progresses forward
Burn-through
A hole melted right through the sheet by the arc
DCEN
DC electrode negative: less heat into the work, shallower penetration
Flare-bevel groove weld
A weld where the rounded bend of a formed section meets a flat surface
Gauge
A number for sheet thickness; the higher the number, the thinner the sheet
Intermittent (stitch) weld
Short welds at set spacing, written length–pitch
Low carbon steel
Mild steel with about 0.25 % carbon or less; welds easily
Metal fume fever
A flu-like illness from breathing zinc and other metal fume
Oil canning
A thin welded panel that bulges and pops in and out when pressed
Peel test
Prising welded sheets apart to check the welds
Pitch
The distance from the centre of one stitch weld to the centre of the next
Plug weld
A weld made in a hole in the top sheet
PQR
Procedure qualification record: the test record that supports a WPS
Weld washer
A thin steel washer on very thin deck so the sheet does not burn away round an arc spot weld
Welding sequence
The planned order and direction of welds on a job
WPQ
Welder performance qualification record: what a welder has passed and is qualified for
WPS
Welding procedure specification: the written instructions for a weld
1G–4G and 1F–4F
AWS position codes for groove and fillet welds: flat, horizontal, vertical, overhead

c1.title: Roof deck for a supermarket in Linstead
c1.text: A crew is fixing galvanised steel roof deck, 0.9 mm thick, to the steel beams of a new supermarket in Linstead, St Catherine, with arc spot welds made to the contractor's WPS. Kemoy, the Level 3 welder leading the crew, is checking the first welds. At one beam the deck has lifted about 3 mm off the steel because of a bent edge. The deck edge is still open on one side of the roof, and it is close to midday.

c2.title: Generator enclosure panels in Cross Roads
c2.text: A shop in Cross Roads, Kingston, is building weatherproof enclosures for small generators from 1.5 mm low carbon steel sheet that arrives with a grey factory primer. The corners are fitted point to point (open corners), and the long butt seams are welded over a copper backing bar. A new welder, Jovan, who has worked only on plate, has burned several holes in the first panel and has once run the arc onto the copper bar.

c3.title: Carport purlins in Mandeville
c3.text: Shanique's team is building a steel carport for a church in Mandeville, Manchester. Galvanised cold-formed channel purlins, 1.5 mm thick, are welded to 6 mm cleats. The drawing calls for flare-bevel groove welds where the rounded bend of each channel meets its cleat, and for 40-120 intermittent fillet welds along a 1 240 mm seam where each purlin laps onto a bracket.

c4.title: A bakery hood in Port Maria
c4.text: At a small shop in Port Maria, St Mary, Oneil is making a canopy hood for a bakery oven from 1.2 mm sheet. After he welded the 1 m × 0.8 m back panel to its frame, running each seam from one end to the other in one go, the panel bulges and pops in and out when it is pressed. Six more hoods of the same design are on order.

c5.title: Fifty medicine cabinets in Falmouth
c5.text: Rushane leads three welders making 50 steel medicine cabinets in 1.5 mm sheet for a clinic in Falmouth, Trelawny, to a WPS that gives 45–65 A for 2.0 mm E6013 electrodes, with flat and vertical seams. One welder, Dwight, has a WPQ for 2 mm sheet in the flat position only, dated March; he has spent the months since on MIG work. It is now November.

questions.q: At the beam where the deck has lifted, the arc burns a ragged hole but the weld does not join the beam. What should Kemoy do?
o: Turn the current up so the arc can reach down to the beam
Press the deck tight onto the beam before making the weld
Fill the hole with extra electrodes until it reaches the beam
Move the weld to the flat part of the deck between the beams
questions.why: An arc spot weld must fuse into the support. With a gap under the sheet, the arc burns the thin deck away before it reaches the beam. The deck is pressed or stood on tight to the beam, as the WPS limits any gap.

questions.q: A peel test on Kemoy's first test piece parts at the weld, leaving a smooth, flat face on the lower piece and no metal torn from the deck. What does this show?
o: The welds are good, as the parts came apart cleanly
The deck is too thick for arc spot welding to the beam
The welds did not fuse properly into the lower piece
The peel test was done wrongly and should be ignored
questions.why: A good arc spot weld tears a button out of the sheet. A clean, flat parting face means the weld sat on the lower piece without fusing into it, so the settings or technique must be put right and the test repeated before production.

questions.q: How should Kemoy check the size of the finished arc spot welds?
o: Count the seconds each one took to make
Tap each one with a hammer and listen to it
Measure each visible weld against the WPS
Look at the colour of the zinc around each one
questions.why: The WPS gives a minimum visible size. Each weld is checked by eye for roundness, edge fusion and cracks, and measured with a rule or gauge; peel tests on trial pieces show the fusion inside.

questions.q: Before any welding is done near the open edge of the deck, which control must be in place first?
o: Edge protection, or harnesses clipped to proper anchors
A second welder to hold the leads clear of the edge
A sun shade over the welder so he can see the arc better
Extra deck sheets stacked along the edge as a barrier
questions.why: A fall from a roof edge can kill. Fall protection is planned before anyone works near an edge, along with shock controls (dry PPE, an insulating mat), fume controls for galvanised deck, and shade and water in the midday heat.

questions.q: The open corners keep burning away. Which change to the fit-up helps most?
o: Widen the gap at each corner so the weld can reach right through
Fit the corners half-open or closed, and weld at a low current
Bevel both edges at 30°, as is done for thick plate
Weld each corner from the inside first, then from the outside
questions.why: Thin edges meeting point to point have nothing to support the pool. Setting one sheet back (half-open) or overlapping it (closed) gives a ledge to weld onto, and less metal is melted, so burn-through stops.

questions.q: How should Jovan mend the holes he has burned in the first panel?
o: Lay a long, slow, wide weave across each hole at full current
Fill each hole with a short piece of electrode core wire, then weld over it
Let it cool, then fill from the edges inward in short dabs at low current
Leave the holes, as the primer and paint will close them up later
questions.why: Heat caused the holes, so more heat makes them bigger. Let the area cool, clean the edges, back the hole if possible, and build up from the edges in short dabs that freeze one by one, then dress and record the repair.

questions.q: Why is it a problem that Jovan ran the arc onto the copper backing bar?
o: Copper melted into the steel weld can make it crack
The copper bar will now be welded on and cannot be removed
Copper makes the slag far harder to chip off the weld
The bar will now carry the current back to the machine
questions.why: A copper bar is only a heat sink and support. If the arc melts it, copper picked up in the steel weld can cause cracking. Keep the joint closed tight on a clean bar and the arc in the joint.

questions.q: The sheet comes with a grey factory primer. What should be done before welding?
o: Weld through it, as primer protects the weld from rust
Turn the current up so the primer burns off in the arc
Wet the primer first so it gives off less smoke in the arc
Remove it from the weld area, unless the WPS allows it
questions.why: Primer gives fume, porosity and poor fusion. It is removed from the weld area, unless the WPS was qualified with that primer left on. Repaint the cleaned area after welding.

questions.q: In the flare-bevel groove welds, where must Shanique's welders make sure the weld fuses?
o: Only on the flat face of the cleat, away from the bend
Only across the top of the curve, to keep the heat off the bend
On the inside of the channel, behind the rounded bend
Right down into the root, where the bend meets the cleat
questions.why: The groove narrows to a root where the rounded bend touches the flat cleat. The weld must fuse right down into it and fill the groove to the drawing's size; a weld that just bridges across the top of the curve is weak.

questions.q: For the 40-120 welds along the 1 240 mm seam, with a weld at each end, what is the total length of weld?
o: 400 mm
440 mm
480 mm
questions.why: Number of welds = (1 240 − 40) ÷ 120 + 1 = 11. Total = 11 × 40 = 440 mm. The gap between welds is 120 − 40 = 80 mm.

questions.q: The welds have burnt the zinc off the galvanised purlins round each joint. What should be done after the welds are inspected?
o: Paint the bare areas with zinc-rich paint
Nothing, as the welds themselves will not rust
Heat the area so the zinc nearby flows back over it
Grind the welds flush so that rain cannot collect on them
questions.why: Bare steel round the welds rusts quickly, especially in wet or salty air. The coating is repaired with zinc-rich paint, as the job specification asks, once the welds have been cleaned and inspected.

questions.q: Which change will do most to stop the back panels of the next hoods from oil canning?
o: Weld each seam end to end in one run at the top of the current range
Use a larger electrode so each seam is finished faster
Tack closely, clamp it and weld short runs in a set order
Leave out the tacks so the panel is free to move as it is welded
questions.why: Oil canning comes from too much heat and shrinkage in one direction. Close tacks, clamping, low heat input and short runs in a balanced sequence spread the shrinkage. A fold or swage in the panel would also stiffen it.

questions.q: Oneil's supervisor tells him to back-step the long seams. What does that mean?
o: Weld short runs, each back towards the last
Weld the whole seam from the far end back towards himself
Weld the seam twice, the second run going the opposite way
Step back from the work between runs to let the fume clear
questions.why: In back-step welding the seam is divided into short lengths. Each run starts a little ahead and is welded back to meet the last one, so the heat and shrinkage are spread along the seam instead of building up at one end.

questions.q: In what order should Oneil tack the next back panel to its frame?
o: All along one long side first, then all along the other side
At the four corners only, so the panel can move as it is welded
Starting at one corner and working round the frame in one direction
From the middle of each side out, opposite sides in turn
questions.why: Tacking from the middle outwards and alternating sides holds the panel evenly and stops the edges creeping or the gaps closing at one end. Close spacing matters too: thin sheet moves easily.

questions.q: What is the position with Dwight's qualification for this job?
o: He is covered for all of it, since a sheet test covers every position
He is covered for the flat seams, as his MIG work keeps it current
He needs only a quick trial weld on the vertical seams to be covered
Flat-only does not cover vertical, and it may have lapsed
questions.why: A flat test generally does not cover vertical work. And a qualification commonly lapses if the welder has not used that process (here MMAW) for six months; MIG work does not keep an MMAW qualification current. Check the code and retest him.

questions.q: How can Rushane best make sure all three welders stay within the 45–65 A range through the run?
o: Ask each welder to report his current at the end of each week
Set every machine dial to 65 A so that no one goes above it
Let each welder set the current he finds runs best on the job
Post the settings and spot-check with a clamp meter
questions.why: Dials are only a guide and differ between machines. Writing the WPS settings at each station and spot-checking the real current with a clamp meter keeps all 50 cabinets to the procedure.

questions.q: A delivery note lists one batch of sheet as 14 gauge and another as 18 gauge. Which batch is thicker?
o: The 18 gauge, by about 0.4 mm
The 14 gauge, by about 0.7 mm
They are the same thickness
The 18 gauge, by about 4 mm
questions.why: The higher the gauge number, the thinner the sheet: 14 gauge is about 1.9 mm and 18 gauge about 1.2 mm. Measure the real thickness with a caliper before setting up.

questions.q: What is the AWS position code for a fillet weld in a lap joint whose sheets stand upright, with the weld running up or down the joint?
o: 2F
3F
3G
4F
questions.why: F is for fillet welds: 1F flat, 2F horizontal, 3F vertical, 4F overhead. G codes (such as 3G) are for groove (butt) welds.

questions.q: On a 1.5 mm cabinet door, a welder strikes his arc on the face of the sheet beside the joint. Why does this matter more than on thick plate?
o: The strike can leave a hole or a hard spot in the thin sheet
The strike makes the electrode coating crack and fall off
The strike makes the machine draw more current from the supply
The strike changes the polarity of the welding circuit
questions.why: An arc strike melts a small spot and cools it very fast. On thin sheet it can go right through or leave a hard, crack-prone spot that shows through the paint. Strike only in the joint.

questions.q: Why is a 0.5 mm deep undercut far more serious on 1.5 mm sheet than on 12 mm plate?
o: Undercut on sheet always grows into a crack within days
Sheet welds are never painted, so undercut cannot be hidden
It takes away about a third of the sheet's thickness
The code allows no undercut at all on plate of any thickness
questions.why: 0.5 mm is a third of 1.5 mm but only about 4 % of 12 mm. On sheet, small faults take away a large share of the strength, so the limits are tight and the sheet technique (low current, short arc, correct angle) matters.
